title: Couinaud Liver Segments
front clue: Hepatic veins split the liver side to side; portal veins split it top from bottom
core concept: The Couinaud system divides the liver into eight functionally independent segments. The three hepatic veins run between segments (interlobar and intersegmental) and divide the liver longitudinally; the right and left portal veins run within segments (intrasegmental) and divide it into superior and inferior tiers. Segment 1 is the caudate lobe, which drains directly into the IVC. Segments 2 (superior) and 3 (inferior) form the left lateral section; segment 4 (4a superior, 4b inferior) is the left medial section. On the right, segments 5 and 8 form the anterior section, and 6 and 7 form the posterior section, with the lower number inferior. The middle hepatic vein and the main lobar fissure, which points to the gallbladder fossa, separate the right and left lobes. The left hepatic vein and the ligamentum teres separate left medial from left lateral. A normal liver measures about 15 to 15.5 cm or less in the midclavicular line, with echogenicity equal to or slightly greater than the right renal cortex.
why it matters: Segment location is how surgeons and radiologists report lesions, so you must translate a described position into a segment number. Remember the numbering runs clockwise from the caudate when viewed from the front, and that within each section the lower number sits inferiorly. Traps: portal veins are intrasegmental, not intersegmental; the falciform ligament and ligamentum teres split the left lobe, not right from left. The caudate's separate venous drainage explains why it is spared and enlarges in Budd-Chiari syndrome and cirrhosis. A Riedel lobe is a normal tongue-like extension of the right lobe, not hepatomegaly.
on the registry: Expect questions asking which structure separates two lobes or sections, which segment a lesion occupies, or which lobe has independent venous drainage into the IVC.
checkpoint: Hepatic veins between segments, portal veins within; caudate is segment 1 and drains straight to the IVC

title: Diffuse Liver Disease
front clue: Bright liver, dark liver, nodular liver: fat, acute hepatitis, cirrhosis
core concept: Fatty infiltration (steatosis) raises liver echogenicity well above the renal cortex, attenuates the beam so the deep liver and diaphragm become hard to see, and blurs the portal vein walls. It can be diffuse, focal, or diffuse with focal sparing; spared areas and focal fat favor the gallbladder fossa, the area anterior to the portal bifurcation, and the caudate lobe, and they show no mass effect and vessels running through them undisplaced. Common causes include obesity, diabetes, alcohol, and steroids. Acute hepatitis may look normal, or the parenchyma may become hypoechoic so that portal triad walls look bright (starry sky), often with gallbladder wall thickening and hepatomegaly. Chronic hepatitis coarsens the echotexture. Cirrhosis shows a nodular surface (best seen with a high-frequency linear probe), coarse heterogeneous parenchyma, atrophy of the right lobe with hypertrophy of the caudate and left lateral segments (caudate to right lobe width ratio above about 0.65), and signs of portal hypertension. Hepatic venous waveforms may lose their normal triphasic pattern and become flat.
why it matters: Pattern recognition is the key skill. A bright, poorly penetrated liver is fat until proven otherwise, but cirrhosis can also look bright, so the surface contour, caudate size, and portal hypertension signs separate them. Do not mistake focal sparing for a hypoechoic mass: look for its typical location, geographic margins, and absence of vessel displacement. Every cirrhotic liver is surveyed for hepatocellular carcinoma, so any new solid nodule matters. Trap: starry sky belongs to acute hepatitis, not to fatty liver, which causes the opposite effect of hiding portal walls.
on the registry: Questions describe echogenicity, penetration, and contour changes and ask for the diffuse process, or ask where focal fatty sparing typically occurs.
checkpoint: Fat hides the portal walls; hepatitis highlights them; cirrhosis makes the surface lumpy

title: Benign Liver Masses
front clue: Bright hemangioma, stealthy FNH with a scar, bleeding adenoma on the pill
core concept: Hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor: a well-defined, homogeneously hyperechoic mass, usually under 3 cm and often subcapsular in the right lobe, with possible posterior enhancement and little detectable internal color flow. Larger ones become heterogeneous. On contrast imaging it shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in. Focal nodular hyperplasia, the second most common benign tumor, is typically seen in women and is often nearly isoechoic to liver (a stealth lesion) with a central scar and spoke-wheel arterial flow radiating from a central artery. Hepatic adenoma occurs in women on oral contraceptives, anabolic steroid users, and glycogen storage disease type I; it is variable in echogenicity and its main danger is hemorrhage and rare malignant transformation, so it is usually resected. A simple hepatic cyst is anechoic and thin walled, with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal flow or contrast enhancement. Pyogenic abscess is complex with debris and possibly gas; amebic abscess is round, hypoechoic, and peripheral near the diaphragm after travel. Echinococcal (hydatid) cysts show daughter cysts or a floating membrane (water lily sign).
why it matters: The exam pairs each mass with a hallmark: hemangioma with hyperechoic and centripetal fill-in, FNH with central scar and spoke-wheel flow, adenoma with oral contraceptives and bleeding. Clinical context separates infections: fever and high white count suggest abscess; travel or exposure to sheep and dogs suggests amebic or hydatid disease. Trap: in a fatty liver, a hemangioma may appear relatively hypoechoic because the background is brighter. Trap two: a hyperechoic lesion in a cirrhotic patient or a cancer patient cannot be assumed to be a hemangioma, because some HCCs and colon metastases are echogenic.
on the registry: Expect a described mass with demographic clues, asking for the most likely benign lesion, its characteristic Doppler or contrast pattern, or its main complication.
checkpoint: Hemangioma bright, FNH scar with spoke wheel, adenoma bleeds

title: Malignant Liver Lesions
front clue: Cirrhosis plus rising AFP: think HCC; multiple targets: think metastases
core concept: Metastases are the most common malignant liver lesions, far outnumbering primary tumors. They are usually multiple and variable: hyperechoic metastases suggest colon, renal cell, or carcinoid primaries; hypoechoic ones suggest breast, lung, or lymphoma; a target or bull's-eye pattern with a hypoechoic halo is a classic appearance; calcified metastases suggest mucinous colon cancer; cystic ones suggest necrosis or cystic primaries. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver malignancy and arises mostly in cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis B or C. It may be solitary, multifocal, or diffusely infiltrative, with variable echogenicity; small lesions are often hypoechoic. Alpha-fetoprotein is frequently elevated. HCC tends to invade the portal vein; tumor thrombus expands the vein and shows arterial-type flow within the thrombus, unlike bland thrombus. Cholangiocarcinoma and hepatoblastoma (young children) are other primaries. Fibrolamellar HCC affects young adults without cirrhosis and has a central scar.
why it matters: Reason from the clinical history. A known primary plus multiple lesions means metastases; cirrhosis or hepatitis B plus a new nodule and rising AFP means HCC until proven otherwise. The single most testable Doppler fact is that tumor thrombus contains arterial flow while bland thrombus does not. Trap: HCC can be hyperechoic and mimic hemangioma, so a bright lesion in a cirrhotic liver needs further characterization. Trap two: a target appearance in the liver is a hallmark of metastasis, whereas a target in the bowel usually means wall thickening.
on the registry: Questions give history and labs (cirrhosis, AFP, known primary) and ask for the diagnosis, the meaning of flow inside a portal vein thrombus, or the most common malignant liver lesion.
checkpoint: Metastases are most common; HCC lives in cirrhosis and invades the portal vein

title: Portal Hypertension and TIPS
front clue: When the liver blocks the road, flow reverses and finds collaterals
core concept: Normal main portal vein flow is hepatopetal (toward the liver), gently phasic with respiration, at roughly 15 to 40 cm/s, and the vein is usually 13 mm or less in diameter. Portal hypertension, most often from cirrhosis, causes a portal vein over 13 mm with lost respiratory variation, slow or to-and-fro flow, and eventually hepatofugal flow. Other signs are splenomegaly, ascites, and portosystemic collaterals: the coronary (left gastric) vein toward esophageal varices, a recanalized paraumbilical vein in the ligamentum teres, splenorenal and short gastric collaterals. Cavernous transformation is a web of collaterals replacing a chronically occluded vein. A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) connects, usually, the right portal vein to the right hepatic vein. With a working TIPS, main portal velocity rises and flow in the intrahepatic portal branches reverses toward the shunt. Commonly cited shunt velocities are about 90 to 190 cm/s; values outside that range, a change of more than 50 cm/s from baseline, or a return to hepatopetal flow in the portal branches suggest dysfunction.
why it matters: Think of portal hypertension as pressure seeking an escape route. Hepatofugal flow and collaterals mean the pressure is high enough to push blood away from the liver. For TIPS, the trap is reversed flow in the left and right portal branches: after TIPS that is expected and healthy, because blood now runs into the low-resistance shunt. Reversion to hepatopetal branch flow is the warning sign. Exact TIPS thresholds vary between institutions, so focus on the trend from the baseline study and on absent flow, which means occlusion.
on the registry: Expect questions on normal portal flow direction, collateral pathways such as the recanalized paraumbilical vein, and what TIPS Doppler findings indicate malfunction.
checkpoint: Hepatofugal plus collaterals means portal hypertension; reversed branch flow after TIPS is normal

title: Liver Transplant Doppler
front clue: In a new liver, the hepatic artery is the lifeline: lose it and the bile ducts die
core concept: The transplanted liver depends on the hepatic artery for biliary blood supply, so hepatic artery thrombosis is the most serious vascular complication, typically early, and it can lead to biliary necrosis, bile leak, and graft loss. Doppler shows absent arterial flow at the porta hepatis and in the liver. Hepatic artery stenosis, usually at the anastomosis, produces a focal velocity elevation (often above about 200 cm/s) with turbulence, and a tardus parvus waveform downstream: slow systolic upstroke, acceleration time over about 0.08 s, and resistive index below 0.5. A normal post-transplant hepatic arterial RI is roughly 0.5 to 0.8; a transiently high RI in the first days is common and usually resolves. Portal vein stenosis or thrombosis, and IVC or hepatic venous anastomotic stenosis, are the other vascular complications. Fluid collections include hematoma, biloma, seroma, and abscess. Rejection has no reliable sonographic sign and is diagnosed by biopsy.
why it matters: Organize transplant Doppler by vessel: artery, portal vein, hepatic veins and IVC. The artery is tested most because its failure threatens the bile ducts. Tardus parvus is the downstream fingerprint of a proximal stenosis, so a low RI with a slow upstroke is more worrying than a high RI. Trap: collateral arteries can develop after thrombosis and produce a weak tardus parvus signal, so faint intrahepatic flow does not exclude a thrombosed main artery. Trap two: do not expect ultrasound to diagnose rejection.
on the registry: Questions present a post-transplant Doppler description and ask for the complication, especially hepatic artery thrombosis or stenosis with tardus parvus.
checkpoint: Transplant artery RI below 0.5 with slow upstroke means look upstream for stenosis

title: Normal Biliary Anatomy
front clue: Fast for the gallbladder; measure the duct inner wall to inner wall
core concept: After a fast of about 6 to 8 hours in adults, the gallbladder is distended, anechoic, and pear shaped, typically up to about 8 to 10 cm long and 4 to 5 cm wide, with a wall of 3 mm or less measured on the anterior wall perpendicular to the beam. It has a fundus, body, neck, and Hartmann pouch; a Phrygian cap is a normal fundal fold. The cystic duct, with its spiral valves of Heister, joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. The common duct lies anterior and lateral to the main portal vein and anterior to the right hepatic artery in the porta hepatis (Mickey Mouse sign), then runs posterolateral in the pancreatic head. Normal common duct diameter is about 6 mm or less, commonly allowing roughly 1 mm more per decade over age 60, and up to about 10 mm after cholecystectomy. Intrahepatic ducts are normally 2 mm or less, or under 40 percent of the adjacent portal vein diameter.
why it matters: Normal values are the yardstick for every biliary question. Measure the duct inner wall to inner wall at its widest point. Use more than one patient position, such as left lateral decubitus and upright, to move stones and resolve folds. Traps: a nonfasting patient has a contracted gallbladder with an apparently thick wall, so check prep before calling wall thickening. A Phrygian cap is a normal variant, not a septum or mass. Age and prior cholecystectomy raise the upper limit for the common duct, so judge dilation in context.
on the registry: Expect questions on normal duct and wall measurements, the relationship of the common duct to the portal vein and hepatic artery, and normal variants such as the Phrygian cap.
checkpoint: Wall 3 mm, duct 6 mm, plus about 1 mm per decade after 60

title: Gallstones and Sludge
front clue: Bright, mobile and shadowing is a stone; layering without a shadow is sludge
core concept: Cholelithiasis is the most common gallbladder disease, with risk factors classically summarized as female, fat, forty, and fertile, plus pregnancy, rapid weight loss, and hemolytic disorders. A typical stone is echogenic, casts a clean posterior acoustic shadow, and moves to the dependent wall when the patient changes position. Shadowing is improved by placing the focal zone at the stone, using a higher frequency, and using harmonic imaging; very small stones may not shadow. A gallbladder packed with stones may show the wall-echo-shadow (WES) sign: the anterior wall, the bright stone surface, then shadow. A stone impacted in the neck does not move and may cause obstruction. Sludge consists of low-level echoes without shadowing that layer dependently and move slowly; it occurs with fasting, total parenteral nutrition, critical illness, and pregnancy. Tumefactive sludge (a sludge ball) can mimic a polyp or mass but has no internal color flow and changes shape or position over time.
why it matters: Mobility and shadowing are the two questions to ask of any echogenic gallbladder focus. Mobile and shadowing equals stone; fixed and nonshadowing suggests a polyp; layering low-level echoes suggest sludge. The WES sign can be confused with bowel gas in the gallbladder fossa; the wall echo in front of the shadow is the clue. Traps: a fold can cast a refraction shadow, and gas in bowel produces a dirty rather than clean shadow. Emphysematous cholecystitis and porcelain gallbladder also cause shadowing from the wall itself.
on the registry: Questions describe an echogenic focus and ask whether it is a stone, polyp, or sludge, or ask how to improve shadowing or what the WES sign represents.
checkpoint: Stone: echogenic, shadows, rolls; sludge: layers, no shadow

title: Acute Cholecystitis
front clue: Stones plus a positive sonographic Murphy sign: the strongest combination
core concept: Acute cholecystitis usually results from a stone obstructing the gallbladder neck or cystic duct. Patients have right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. The two most predictive findings are gallstones and a positive sonographic Murphy sign, meaning maximal tenderness when the transducer presses directly over the gallbladder; together they carry a high positive predictive value. Supporting findings include wall thickening over 3 mm, often with a striated or hypoechoic layered wall, pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, an impacted stone, and wall hyperemia. Complications include gangrenous cholecystitis, with asymmetric wall thickening, intraluminal membranes, and a Murphy sign that may be absent because of nerve necrosis; emphysematous cholecystitis, with gas in the wall or lumen producing bright echoes and dirty shadowing or ring-down, more common in diabetics; and perforation, with a wall defect and pericholecystic abscess. Acalculous cholecystitis affects critically ill patients such as those in intensive care or after trauma or burns. Chronic cholecystitis shows a small, contracted, thick-walled gallbladder with stones.
why it matters: Wall thickening alone is nonspecific: hepatitis, ascites, heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, and a postprandial state all thicken the wall. That is why stones and a focal Murphy sign carry more weight. Always perform the Murphy sign yourself before the patient gets pain medication, because analgesia blunts it. Trap: a negative Murphy sign does not exclude disease if the gallbladder is gangrenous. Trap two: gas in the wall can be mistaken for a porcelain gallbladder or bowel; ring-down artifact and clinical toxicity point to emphysematous cholecystitis, a surgical emergency.
on the registry: Expect a clinical vignette with RUQ pain and findings described in words, asking for the most specific sign, the complication present, or the cause of a thick wall without inflammation.
checkpoint: Stones plus focal Murphy beat wall thickness alone

title: Gallbladder Wall Lesions
front clue: Comet tails mean adenomyomatosis; fixed, nonshadowing bumps are polyps
core concept: Adenomyomatosis is a benign hyperplastic condition in which mucosa herniates into a thickened muscular wall, forming Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. Cholesterol crystals in these sinuses create bright foci with V-shaped comet-tail reverberation artifact on gray scale and often twinkling artifact on color Doppler. It may be diffuse, segmental (hourglass narrowing), or focal at the fundus. Gallbladder polyps are fixed, nonshadowing, nonmobile projections from the wall; most are cholesterol polyps, and they may show a small feeding vessel. Size and shape drive management. The classic teaching is surgical referral at 10 mm or larger. The 2022 SRU consensus stratifies by morphology: extremely low risk polyps (pedunculated ball-on-the-wall or thin stalk) need no follow-up up to 9 mm, ultrasound follow-up at 6, 12 and 24 months for 10 to 14 mm, and surgical consultation at 15 mm or more; low risk polyps (sessile or broad-based) need no follow-up up to 6 mm, follow-up at 12 months for 7 to 9 mm, follow-up or surgical consultation for 10 to 14 mm, and surgical consultation at 15 mm or more. Adjacent focal wall thickening of 4 mm or more, or growth of 4 mm or more within 12 months, prompts surgical consultation. Gallbladder carcinoma is associated with gallstones, chronic inflammation, and porcelain gallbladder (wall calcification). It appears as a mass replacing the gallbladder lumen, focal or diffuse irregular wall thickening, or an intraluminal mass with internal flow, often invading the adjacent liver and causing biliary obstruction at the porta hepatis.
why it matters: The two key separations are polyp versus stone (fixed and nonshadowing versus mobile and shadowing) and polyp versus tumefactive sludge (internal flow and fixed position versus avascular and shifting). Comet-tail artifact from the wall is reassuring because it signals adenomyomatosis. Exact polyp follow-up thresholds have changed with recent consensus, so learn the classic 10 mm rule while recognizing that morphology now matters. Trap: a porcelain gallbladder can look like a stone-filled gallbladder because of the curvilinear shadowing wall, and both carry different implications for cancer risk.
on the registry: Questions describe a wall finding with or without comet tails, mobility, or flow, and ask for the diagnosis or the size that prompts surgical referral.
checkpoint: Comet tail in the wall is adenomyomatosis; 10 mm polyp is the classic surgical threshold

title: Biliary Obstruction
front clue: Find where the ducts stop dilating: that is where the problem lives
core concept: Obstructive jaundice raises direct (conjugated) bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT. Dilated intrahepatic ducts run parallel to portal veins, producing the parallel channel (shotgun) sign. The level of obstruction is found where dilated ducts become normal. Choledocholithiasis is the most common cause; distal duct stones may lack shadowing and are often obscured by duodenal gas. Distal obstruction from a pancreatic head or ampullary mass dilates both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct (double-duct sign); Courvoisier sign is a painless, palpable, nontender enlarged gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignant obstruction rather than stone disease. Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Klatskin tumor) dilates intrahepatic ducts that fail to join at the confluence, with a normal-caliber common duct. Mirizzi syndrome is a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct, dilating ducts above it with a normal duct below. A choledochal cyst, most commonly Todani type I fusiform dilation of the common duct, is a congenital cyst separate from the gallbladder, usually found in children.
why it matters: Localizing obstruction is the reasoning skill being tested. Dilated intrahepatic ducts with a normal common duct point to the hilum (Klatskin or Mirizzi); dilated common and pancreatic ducts point to the pancreatic head or ampulla. Painless jaundice with a big gallbladder suggests cancer; painful jaundice with a small gallbladder suggests stones, since chronic inflammation prevents distension. Trap: dilated ducts can mimic vessels, so always use color Doppler. Trap two: a choledochal cyst can be mistaken for a duodenal or pancreatic cyst unless you show it communicating with the ducts.
on the registry: Expect scenarios with jaundice and lab values asking for the level of obstruction, the meaning of Courvoisier sign, or the diagnosis behind a described pattern of duct dilation.
checkpoint: Painless jaundice plus a big gallbladder is cancer until proven otherwise

title: Pancreatic Anatomy
front clue: Find the splenic vein and you have found the back of the pancreas
core concept: The pancreas is a retroperitoneal gland lying in the anterior pararenal space, identified mainly by its vascular landmarks. The splenic vein runs along the posterior body and tail and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal confluence. The head sits in the duodenal C-loop, to the right of the SMV and anterior to the IVC; the uncinate process tucks posterior to the SMV. The neck lies anterior to the SMV and portal confluence, the body anterior to the SMA and aorta, and the tail extends toward the splenic hilum. The gastroduodenal artery marks the anterolateral head and the common bile duct the posterolateral head. Approximate upper limits are 3 cm for the head and 2.5 cm for the body and tail, with a main duct (duct of Wirsung) of about 3 mm or less. Echogenicity increases with age as fat replaces tissue: the gland is relatively hypoechoic in children and equal to or more echogenic than the liver in adults.
why it matters: Most pancreatic questions are really vascular landmark questions. Learn the transverse picture: SMV to the left of the head, SMA behind the SMV, aorta behind the SMA, IVC behind the head. The GDA is anterior and the CBD posterior in the head, an easy pair to reverse under pressure. Trap: an echogenic pancreas in an older adult is usually normal fatty replacement, not chronic pancreatitis. Trap two: the splenic vein marks the posterior border of the body and tail; peripancreatic fluid tracking between the gland and the splenic vein lies in the anterior pararenal space, whereas fluid anterior to the pancreas, behind the stomach, is in the lesser sac. Fill the stomach with water to improve the window.
on the registry: Questions ask which vessel lies posterior to a pancreatic part, which structures mark the anterior and posterior head, and how echogenicity changes with age.
checkpoint: GDA anterior, CBD posterior; splenic vein behind the body and tail; uncinate tucks behind the SMV

title: Acute Pancreatitis
front clue: Gallstones and alcohol light the fire; lipase confirms it
core concept: Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory process most often caused by gallstones or alcohol; other causes include hypertriglyceridemia, trauma, ERCP, drugs, and hypercalcemia. Patients present with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting, with elevated serum amylase and lipase; lipase stays elevated longer and is more specific. The pancreas may look normal in mild disease. Otherwise it is diffusely enlarged and hypoechoic from edema, with poorly defined margins and peripancreatic fluid, often in the lesser sac and anterior pararenal space. Focal pancreatitis can mimic a mass. The main role of ultrasound is to look for gallstones and biliary dilation, which change management, because CT better stages severity. Under the revised Atlanta classification, early collections are acute peripancreatic fluid collections or acute necrotic collections; after about four weeks, they become a pseudocyst or walled-off necrosis. Vascular complications include splenic vein thrombosis and splenic artery pseudoaneurysm, which shows swirling yin-yang color flow inside a cystic-appearing mass.
why it matters: The exam expects you to know that a normal-looking pancreas does not exclude pancreatitis, and that finding gallstones is the most important sonographic contribution. Bowel gas from ileus often limits the exam, so expect a suboptimal window. Trap: never assume a cystic mass near an inflamed pancreas is a simple pseudocyst; check it with color Doppler first, because a pseudoaneurysm looks cystic in gray scale and needle drainage would be dangerous. Trap two: amylase rises and falls quickly, so a late presentation may show only an elevated lipase.
on the registry: Questions present epigastric pain and lab values and ask for the diagnosis, the most specific enzyme, the expected appearance, or the dangerous complication to exclude with Doppler.
checkpoint: Edematous, enlarged, hypoechoic; always look for stones and check cysts with color

title: Chronic Pancreatitis and Pseudocyst
front clue: Calcified, shrunken and beaded: years of alcohol written in the gland
core concept: Chronic pancreatitis results from repeated inflammation, most often from alcohol, causing irreversible fibrosis and loss of exocrine and endocrine function, with chronic pain, malabsorption and steatorrhea, and diabetes. Sonographically the gland is small, heterogeneous, and echogenic with irregular margins. Parenchymal and intraductal calcifications are the most specific finding and may shadow. The main pancreatic duct is dilated and beaded or irregular, sometimes containing stones. Pseudocysts are common, and the disease raises the risk of adenocarcinoma, which can be hard to separate from a focal inflammatory mass. A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic fluid enclosed by a fibrous wall without an epithelial lining, which takes about four weeks to form after acute pancreatitis. It is usually anechoic or contains debris, has a well-defined wall, and most often sits in the lesser sac, though it can track into the mediastinum, spleen, or pelvis. Complications include infection, hemorrhage, rupture, and compression of the bile duct or stomach.
why it matters: Separate the echogenic gland of normal aging from chronic pancreatitis by looking for calcifications and an irregular dilated duct; atrophy alone is not enough. Pseudocysts are named for their missing epithelial lining, a common recall point. Trap: a cystic mass in a patient with no history of pancreatitis should not be called a pseudocyst, because a cystic neoplasm is possible. Trap two: hemorrhage or infection gives a pseudocyst internal echoes, so it can resemble a solid or complex mass; look for posterior enhancement and the absence of internal flow.
on the registry: Expect questions on the most specific sign of chronic pancreatitis, the definition and timing of pseudocyst formation, and the most common pseudocyst location.
checkpoint: Calcifications plus a beaded duct is chronic pancreatitis; a pseudocyst has no epithelial lining

title: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma
front clue: Painless jaundice, a hypoechoic head mass, and two dilated ducts
core concept: Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common pancreatic neoplasm and carries a poor prognosis. Risk factors include smoking, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, and family history; the tumor marker CA 19-9 is often elevated. About two thirds arise in the head. Head tumors present early with painless jaundice and weight loss, while body and tail tumors present late with pain and metastases. The typical appearance is an ill-defined, hypoechoic, solid mass with little internal flow. Head lesions obstruct both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct (double-duct sign) and may produce a large, nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). The scan must assess resectability and spread: encasement or invasion of the SMA, SMV, portal vein, or celiac axis, liver metastases, peripancreatic and periportal lymph nodes, and ascites. Atrophy of the gland upstream of the tumor with a dilated duct is a secondary sign that a small mass is present.
why it matters: The exam asks you to connect the clinical picture to the location: painless jaundice localizes to the head. A dilated pancreatic duct without an obvious cause should prompt a careful search of the head and uncinate process. Staging questions focus on vessels, because SMA encasement generally makes the tumor unresectable. Trap: focal acute or chronic pancreatitis can also make a hypoechoic head mass, so history and labs matter. Trap two: ampullary and distal bile duct tumors also cause a double-duct sign, so it points to a location, not one specific tumor.
on the registry: Questions present painless jaundice and weight loss, then ask for the likely diagnosis, location, associated sign, or vascular involvement that matters for staging.
checkpoint: Hypoechoic head mass plus double ducts plus Courvoisier is the classic triad

title: Pancreatic Cystic and Neuroendocrine Tumors
front clue: Grandmother serous, mother mucinous, daughter pseudopapillary, grandfather IPMN
core concept: Serous cystadenoma is a benign tumor of older women, usually in the head, composed of many tiny cysts that can look solid or honeycomb-like, often with a central stellate scar that may calcify. Mucinous cystic neoplasm occurs in middle-aged women, usually in the body or tail, and has fewer, larger cysts (macrocystic) with thick septa or mural nodules; it has malignant potential and is resected. Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) is typical of older men and communicates with the pancreatic duct; main-duct IPMN, with a markedly dilated main duct, carries the highest malignant risk, while branch-duct IPMN appears as cysts connected to side branches. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm affects young women and is a mixed solid and cystic mass, often hemorrhagic. Neuroendocrine (islet cell) tumors are well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, and hypervascular. Insulinoma is the most common functioning type and is usually small, causing hypoglycemia; gastrinoma causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and sits in the gastrinoma triangle. Multiple tumors suggest MEN 1.
why it matters: The age and sex mnemonic plus location and cyst size answers most items. Microcystic and central scar means serous and benign; macrocystic in the tail of a middle-aged woman means mucinous and needs surgery. Duct communication is the defining feature of IPMN. Trap: a pseudocyst is the most common pancreatic cyst overall, so history matters, but a septated cyst with nodules is not a pseudocyst. Trap two: neuroendocrine tumors are hypervascular, which helps separate them from the hypovascular adenocarcinoma.
on the registry: Expect a vignette giving age, sex, location, and cyst morphology, asking for the most likely neoplasm, which lesion communicates with the duct, or which syndrome a functioning tumor causes.
checkpoint: Microcystic and scar is serous; macrocystic tail is mucinous; duct connection is IPMN

title: Normal Spleen and Variants
front clue: A round nodule by the splenic hilum that matches the spleen is a splenule
core concept: The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ in the left upper quadrant, part of the reticuloendothelial system, that filters blood, removes old red cells, and contributes to immunity. Its normal length is usually quoted as up to about 12 to 13 cm in adults. It is homogeneous and slightly more echogenic than or equal to the normal liver, and more echogenic than the kidney. The splenic artery arises from the celiac trunk and the splenic vein exits the hilum to run behind the pancreas. An accessory spleen (splenule) is the most common variant, found in roughly 10 to 30 percent of people, usually near the splenic hilum or tail of pancreas. It is round, smooth, under about 2 to 3 cm, isoechoic to the spleen, and supplied by a splenic artery branch. After splenectomy, splenules can enlarge. Other variants include a wandering spleen on a long pedicle, at risk of torsion, and the asplenia and polysplenia heterotaxy syndromes, often with congenital heart disease.
why it matters: The practical skill is recognizing a splenule so it is not called a lymph node, adrenal mass, or pancreatic tail tumor. Matching echogenicity to the spleen and a vessel from the splenic artery are the clues. Measure the spleen in its longest axis, usually from a coronal intercostal view with the patient in the right lateral decubitus position. Trap: the left lobe of a large liver can wrap around the spleen and mimic a subcapsular collection. Trap two: splenules matter after splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia, because they can cause the disease to recur.
on the registry: Questions ask for normal splenic length and echogenicity, the most common splenic variant and its location, or how to tell a splenule from a lymph node.
checkpoint: Splenule: round, hilar, and isoechoic to the spleen

title: Splenomegaly
front clue: Big spleen: think congestion, infection, blood cancer, or storage disease
core concept: Splenomegaly is generally defined as a length above about 12 to 13 cm, or an inferior tip extending below the lower pole of the left kidney, or a spleen that wraps anteriorly over the left kidney. Causes group into categories. Congestive: portal hypertension from cirrhosis, splenic or portal vein thrombosis, and right heart failure. Infectious: mononucleosis, malaria, bacterial endocarditis, and other systemic infections. Hematologic and neoplastic: leukemia, lymphoma, myelofibrosis, hemolytic anemias, and polycythemia vera. Infiltrative and storage: Gaucher disease and amyloidosis. Massive splenomegaly is classically seen with chronic myelogenous leukemia, myelofibrosis, malaria, and Gaucher disease. In sickle cell disease the spleen may enlarge in childhood and then shrink and calcify through repeated infarction (autosplenectomy). An enlarged spleen is more vulnerable to rupture, which is why patients with mononucleosis are told to avoid contact sports. Echotexture is usually homogeneous, so look for focal lesions, collateral vessels at the hilum, and liver disease to narrow the cause.
why it matters: When you see a large spleen, scan for the cause: a nodular liver and portosystemic collaterals point to portal hypertension, while lymphadenopathy suggests lymphoma. Clinical clues such as a young adult with sore throat and fatigue point to mononucleosis. Trap: an elongated spleen with normal volume can exceed 13 cm in tall people, so use the relationship to the kidney and the overall shape too. Trap two: sickle cell disease produces a large spleen in young children but a small, echogenic, calcified spleen in adults.
on the registry: Expect questions asking for the most common cause of splenomegaly in a described patient, the causes of massive enlargement, or why contact sports are restricted in mononucleosis.
checkpoint: Congestion, infection, hematologic disease, storage: four bins for a big spleen

title: Splenic Infarct and Trauma
front clue: Wedge pointing to the hilum is an infarct; left shoulder pain after trauma is Kehr
core concept: A splenic infarct results from occlusion of a splenic artery branch, from emboli (endocarditis, atrial fibrillation), sickle cell disease, splenomegaly, vasculitis, or hypercoagulable states. It typically appears as a peripheral, wedge-shaped hypoechoic area with the base at the capsule and the apex toward the hilum, without color flow; with time it becomes more echogenic and contracts, and it can be round or multiple. The spleen is among the most commonly injured solid organs in blunt abdominal trauma. Injuries include subcapsular hematoma (a crescent of fluid flattening the splenic contour), intraparenchymal hematoma, laceration (a linear or irregular hypoechoic or heterogeneous defect), and rupture with hemoperitoneum. Fresh blood can be echogenic and nearly isoechoic to spleen, then becomes hypoechoic or complex as it evolves. The FAST exam looks for free fluid in the left upper quadrant (splenorenal space), right upper quadrant (Morison pouch), and pelvis. Left shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation by blood is the Kehr sign. Delayed rupture of a subcapsular hematoma can occur days later.
why it matters: Shape is the key clue for infarct: wedge-shaped and peripheral, pointing to the hilum, because that is the territory of an end artery. In trauma, the exam emphasizes free fluid over organ detail, since CT grades the injury; free fluid in a hypotensive trauma patient is the critical finding. Trap: acute hematoma can be isoechoic to the spleen and easily missed, so look for contour bulges and perisplenic fluid. Trap two: lack of a laceration on ultrasound does not exclude splenic injury.
on the registry: Questions describe a wedge-shaped lesion in a patient with emboli, or a trauma patient with left shoulder pain and perisplenic fluid, and ask for the diagnosis or sign.
checkpoint: Wedge with base at the capsule means infarct; Kehr sign means blood under the left diaphragm

title: Focal Splenic Lesions
front clue: Tiny bright dots are old granulomas; dark nodules in a big spleen suggest lymphoma
core concept: Splenic cysts may be true epithelial (congenital) cysts, which are anechoic and may contain thin septa, or post-traumatic pseudocysts, which lack an epithelial lining and often have calcified walls and internal echoes. Echinococcal cysts occur in endemic areas. Hemangioma is the most common benign splenic neoplasm, usually echogenic, and hamartoma is a rarer solid lesion. Multiple small echogenic foci, with or without shadowing, are typical of calcified granulomas from prior histoplasmosis or tuberculosis. In portal hypertension, small echogenic Gamna-Gandy bodies from old hemorrhage can appear. Lymphoma is the most common malignancy of the spleen; it may cause homogeneous splenomegaly or multiple hypoechoic nodules, sometimes nearly anechoic, that can mimic cysts but have no posterior enhancement or have internal flow. Metastases to the spleen are uncommon, classically from melanoma, breast, and lung. Splenic abscesses occur in immunocompromised patients and intravenous drug users, and fungal microabscesses can give a target or wheel-within-a-wheel appearance.
why it matters: Reason by echogenicity and number. Bright, tiny, and multiple means old granulomatous disease and is usually incidental. Hypoechoic and multiple in a patient with lymphadenopathy or B symptoms suggests lymphoma. Near-anechoic lymphoma is a classic trap, because it can look like cysts; look for the lack of a clean back wall and lack of strong posterior enhancement. Fever plus a complex lesion in an immunocompromised patient points to abscess. Remember the spleen is an unusual site for metastases, so a solitary solid lesion is more often benign.
on the registry: Expect a described lesion pattern, asking for the most likely diagnosis: granulomas, lymphoma, cyst type, hemangioma, or abscess.
checkpoint: Bright dots are granulomas; lymphoma is the top splenic malignancy

title: Normal Kidney and Congenital Variants
front clue: Pseudotumors are made of normal cortex; fused poles sit in front of the aorta
core concept: The adult kidney measures about 10 to 12 cm long, 4 to 6 cm wide, and 2.5 to 4 cm thick, with the two sides normally within about 2 cm of each other. The cortex is hypoechoic or isoechoic to the normal liver and spleen, the medullary pyramids are hypoechoic (especially prominent in neonates), and the central renal sinus is echogenic from fat. Normal variants that mimic masses include the column of Bertin (cortex extending into the sinus), the dromedary hump (a bulge of the left lateral cortex beneath the spleen), and the junctional parenchymal defect (an echogenic triangular notch, usually anterior upper pole). A horseshoe kidney is fused at the lower poles by an isthmus lying anterior to the aorta and IVC, held low by the inferior mesenteric artery, and prone to obstruction and stones. A duplex collecting system obeys the Weigert-Meyer rule: the upper pole ureter inserts inferomedially and tends to obstruct, often with an ectopic ureterocele, while the lower pole ureter tends to reflux. Ectopic kidneys are most often pelvic.
why it matters: The exam often hides a normal variant behind a mass-like description, so ask whether the tissue matches normal cortex in echogenicity and vascular pattern. If it does, it is a pseudotumor. When a kidney is missing from the renal fossa, look in the pelvis and across the midline before calling agenesis. The Weigert-Meyer rule is a favorite: upper pole obstructs, lower pole refluxes. Trap: the isthmus of a horseshoe kidney can be mistaken for a para-aortic lymph node or mass. Trap two: prominent neonatal pyramids are normal, not hydronephrosis or cysts.
on the registry: Questions ask for normal renal size and echogenicity, identify a pseudotumor from a description, or test the Weigert-Meyer rule and horseshoe kidney anatomy.
checkpoint: Upper pole ureter obstructs, lower pole refluxes; horseshoe isthmus sits under the IMA
