title: Renal Cysts and Bosniak
front clue: Simple cyst: anechoic, thin wall, bright back wall; anything more climbs the Bosniak ladder
core concept: A simple renal cyst is very common with age and meets three criteria: anechoic, a thin smooth imperceptible wall, and posterior acoustic enhancement. It needs no follow-up. The Bosniak classification, developed for CT and updated for CT and MRI in 2019, stratifies complex cysts. Category I is simple. Category II has a few thin septa, thin calcification, or uniformly hyperattenuating content, and is benign. Category IIF has more numerous or minimally thickened smooth septa and requires follow-up imaging. Category III has thickened or irregular enhancing walls or septa and roughly half are malignant. Category IV contains enhancing soft tissue nodules and most are malignant. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound can characterize enhancement. Parapelvic cysts sit in the sinus and must not be mistaken for hydronephrosis. Polycystic disease includes autosomal dominant PKD (enlarged kidneys with innumerable cysts, liver cysts, berry aneurysms) and autosomal recessive PKD (enlarged echogenic infant kidneys). Dialysis patients develop acquired cystic disease and an increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.
why it matters: Think of the Bosniak ladder as asking one question: how much enhancing tissue is there? More soft tissue means more malignancy risk. On ultrasound, internal flow in a septum or nodule is the equivalent of enhancement. Trap: parapelvic cysts are separate, noncommunicating, and do not connect to a dilated pelvis or ureter, unlike hydronephrosis. Trap two: ultrasound overestimates septal thickness and internal echoes compared with CT, so a complex appearance often needs CT, MRI, or CEUS rather than an immediate diagnosis. ADPKD is inherited and adult; ARPKD presents in infancy.
on the registry: Expect questions on simple cyst criteria, which Bosniak category needs follow-up or surgery, polycystic disease associations, and cysts that mimic hydronephrosis.
checkpoint: Anechoic, thin wall, enhancement: simple; enhancing nodule: Bosniak IV

title: Hydronephrosis and Urolithiasis
front clue: Connected anechoic spaces in the sinus mean obstruction; twinkling means stone
core concept: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces, usually from obstruction. The dilated spaces are anechoic and branch into one connected pelvis. Grading runs from mild (pelvis and calyces mildly dilated) to moderate (rounded calyces) to severe (marked dilation with cortical thinning). False positives include an overdistended bladder, an extrarenal pelvis, parapelvic cysts, prominent renal vessels (use color), and reflux. Causes include stones, UPJ obstruction, pregnancy, tumors, retroperitoneal fibrosis, and bladder outlet obstruction such as an enlarged prostate. Renal stones are echogenic with posterior shadowing; on color Doppler many show twinkling artifact, a rapidly changing color signal behind a rough reflector. Ureteral stones lodge at three narrow points: the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the ureterovesical junction, which is the most common site. Ureteral jets seen with color in the bladder suggest at least partial patency; an absent jet on one side supports obstruction. An intrarenal resistive index above about 0.70 may support acute obstruction but is nonspecific.
why it matters: Most stone and obstruction questions combine anatomy and artifacts. Use color to confirm that a dilated sinus is not vascular and twinkling to confirm a stone. Asymmetric ureteral jets are a functional clue. Trap: hydronephrosis may be absent in very early obstruction or with dehydration, so a normal collecting system does not completely exclude a stone. Trap two: check the bladder before calling hydronephrosis, because an overfull bladder can dilate both systems; rescan after voiding. Severity correlates with cortical thinning, which signals chronic obstruction.
on the registry: Questions describe dilation, shadowing, twinkling, or jets and ask for the diagnosis, the most common stone site, or the cause of a false-positive hydronephrosis.
checkpoint: UVJ is the most common stone site; twinkling helps confirm a stone

title: Medical Renal Disease
front clue: Bright cortex brighter than liver means the kidney itself is sick
core concept: Renal failure is classified as prerenal (reduced perfusion, such as dehydration or heart failure), intrinsic renal (glomerular, tubular, or interstitial disease, such as acute tubular necrosis or glomerulonephritis), and postrenal (obstruction). Labs show rising BUN and creatinine and a falling glomerular filtration rate. The main role of ultrasound is to exclude obstruction, because postrenal failure is treatable, and to judge chronicity. In acute intrinsic disease the kidneys may be normal or enlarged, sometimes with increased cortical echogenicity. Medical renal disease is suggested when cortical echogenicity is greater than that of the normal liver or spleen, especially with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Chronic kidney disease produces small (usually under about 9 cm), echogenic kidneys with thin cortex, often with acquired cysts after dialysis. Common chronic causes are diabetes and hypertension; diabetic kidneys may remain normal in size until late. Acute pyelonephritis may look normal or show an enlarged kidney, areas of altered echogenicity, and reduced perfusion; emphysematous pyelonephritis shows gas.
why it matters: Compare cortex to liver at the same depth, and make sure the liver itself is normal, because a fatty liver can make a sick kidney look normal by comparison. Small, bright kidneys mean chronic disease, which means a biopsy is less useful and recovery less likely. Trap: increased echogenicity indicates disease but does not name a specific cause. Trap two: echogenicity tells you little about function; a kidney can look normal in significant acute failure. Always image the bladder and look for hydronephrosis to rule out the postrenal cause first.
on the registry: Expect questions asking why ultrasound is ordered for renal failure, what echogenic small kidneys mean, or which category a given cause belongs to.
checkpoint: Rule out obstruction first; small and bright means chronic

title: Solid Renal Masses
front clue: Very bright and shadowing suggests fat-filled AML; solid and vascular in a smoker suggests RCC
core concept: Angiomyolipoma is the most common benign solid renal tumor, composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat. Because of its fat content it is typically very hyperechoic, often as bright as the renal sinus, and may show posterior shadowing. Multiple bilateral AMLs suggest tuberous sclerosis. Larger lesions, commonly over about 4 cm, carry a risk of spontaneous hemorrhage. Because small renal cell carcinomas can also be echogenic, CT or MRI is used to confirm macroscopic fat. Renal cell carcinoma is the most common adult renal malignancy, more frequent in men, smokers, obese patients, dialysis patients, and von Hippel-Lindau disease. Classic triad: hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass, though most are now incidental. RCC is usually a solid mass that is isoechoic or hypoechoic, and often shows internal flow. It tends to invade the renal vein and IVC, so these must be examined. A new left varicocele can signal left renal vein obstruction. Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma arises in the collecting system as a hypoechoic sinus mass.
why it matters: The decision point is whether an echogenic mass is AML or something more dangerous. Brightness similar to sinus fat and shadowing favor AML, but cannot exclude RCC, so further imaging follows. Always follow a solid renal mass into the renal vein and IVC. Trap: Wilms tumor is the pediatric counterpart of RCC, so age matters in the question. Trap two: a hypoechoic mass in the renal sinus splaying the sinus fat suggests urothelial carcinoma rather than RCC. Remember tuberous sclerosis whenever you see multiple bilateral AMLs.
on the registry: Questions describe a renal mass with demographics or syndromes and ask for the most likely tumor, its risk, or which vessel must be evaluated next.
checkpoint: AML is bright fat that can bleed; RCC goes for the renal vein and IVC

title: Renal Transplant Complications
front clue: Time since surgery tells you which fluid collection you are looking at
core concept: A renal transplant is placed extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa, usually the right, with the renal artery anastomosed to the external iliac artery and the ureter implanted into the bladder. Fluid collections are timed: hematoma and urinoma appear early, urinoma typically in the first weeks, lymphocele is the most common, usually 4 to 8 weeks after surgery, often septated, and may compress the ureter causing hydronephrosis; abscess presents with fever. Acute tubular necrosis is the most common cause of early delayed graft function, especially with deceased donors. Rejection may cause an enlarged graft, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and an elevated resistive index (above about 0.8), but these findings are nonspecific and biopsy is diagnostic. Renal vein thrombosis typically shows absent venous flow and reversed diastolic flow in the renal artery. Transplant renal artery stenosis shows high velocities at the anastomosis (often over about 200 to 250 cm/s) and tardus parvus downstream. An arteriovenous fistula after biopsy shows high-velocity, low-resistance flow and perivascular tissue vibration artifact.
why it matters: Sort transplant problems into vascular, collecting system, fluid collections, and parenchymal dysfunction, then use timing. Reversed diastolic arterial flow with no venous signal is the signature of renal vein thrombosis and is an emergency. Trap: an elevated RI does not diagnose rejection; ATN, obstruction, compression by a collection, and drug toxicity all raise it. Trap two: a lymphocele can look like a bladder diverticulum or hydroureter, so trace its connections and check its timing. Mild collecting system fullness is common in transplants and must be compared with prior studies.
on the registry: Expect a described Doppler waveform or collection with postoperative timing, asking for the complication: renal vein thrombosis, stenosis, lymphocele, ATN, or AV fistula.
checkpoint: Reversed arterial diastole with absent venous flow means graft renal vein thrombosis

title: Bladder and Adrenal Masses
front clue: A fixed, vascular bladder mass is tumor; a moving, avascular one is clot
core concept: The distended bladder wall is normally about 3 mm or less, and up to about 5 mm when less full; diffuse thickening suggests cystitis or outlet obstruction with trabeculation. Bladder volume and post-void residual are commonly calculated as length times width times height times about 0.52. Urothelial carcinoma is the most common bladder malignancy, usually presenting with painless hematuria; it is a fixed, irregular wall mass with internal flow. Blood clots and debris are mobile and avascular, and bladder stones are mobile and shadowing. A ureterocele is a cystic dilation of the distal ureter in the bladder (cobra head); a diverticulum is an outpouching with a neck. The adrenal glands sit superomedial to the kidneys; the right lies posterior to the IVC and the left lateral to the aorta. Adenoma is the most common adrenal mass. Myelolipoma contains fat and is very echogenic. Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension and elevated metanephrines. Neonatal adrenal hemorrhage is the most common neonatal adrenal mass, while neuroblastoma is a solid, often calcified childhood tumor.
why it matters: For any bladder mass, ask whether it moves and whether it has flow: tumors are fixed and vascular. Reposition the patient to demonstrate mobility. Adrenal questions hinge on age and lab clues: hypertension episodes with headache and sweating point to pheochromocytoma; a neonate after a difficult delivery points to hemorrhage, which shrinks and changes on follow-up, unlike neuroblastoma, which grows. Trap: a right adrenal mass can be confused with the upper pole of the kidney or the crus of the diaphragm. Trap two: bladder wall thickness must be judged with adequate distension.
on the registry: Questions describe a bladder or adrenal mass with mobility, Doppler, age, or lab clues and ask for the diagnosis or the volume formula.
checkpoint: Bladder mass: fixed plus flow equals tumor; neonatal adrenal mass is usually hemorrhage

title: Aorta and Visceral Branches
front clue: Celiac seagull first, SMA in its fat collar next, renals off the sides
core concept: The abdominal aorta enters through the diaphragmatic hiatus and tapers toward its bifurcation into the common iliac arteries at about the level of the umbilicus (L4). Normal diameter is under 3 cm, measured outer wall to outer wall perpendicular to its long axis. The first anterior branch is the celiac trunk, about 1 to 2 cm below the diaphragm, which divides into the common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries (the seagull or T sign in transverse view). The superior mesenteric artery arises about 1 cm below the celiac and runs parallel and anterior to the aorta, surrounded by echogenic fat. The left renal vein passes between the SMA and aorta to reach the IVC; compression there is the nutcracker phenomenon. The renal arteries arise laterally, just below the SMA; the right renal artery passes posterior to the IVC. The celiac trunk and renal arteries have low-resistance flow with continuous diastolic flow. The fasting SMA is high resistance, often triphasic, and becomes low resistance after a meal.
why it matters: Branch order and the waveform logic behind it are the core tested facts. Organs that need constant flow, such as the liver, spleen, and kidneys, are fed by low-resistance arteries; the fasting bowel does not, so the SMA is high resistance until a meal opens up the mesenteric bed. Trap: the right renal artery, not the left renal vein, runs behind the IVC. Trap two: measure the aorta perpendicular to the vessel, not the body, since a tortuous aorta measured obliquely looks falsely enlarged. Use these landmarks to find the pancreas.
on the registry: Questions ask for the order of branches, which vessel passes between the SMA and aorta, which branch is high resistance when fasting, and how to measure the aorta.
checkpoint: Low resistance feeds constant demand; fasting SMA is high resistance until you eat

title: Aortic Aneurysm and Dissection
front clue: 3 cm makes it an aneurysm; 5.5 cm in a man usually means repair
core concept: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is an aortic diameter of 3 cm or more, or at least 1.5 times the normal proximal diameter. Most are infrarenal, fusiform, and atherosclerotic; saccular aneurysms are focal outpouchings and more often mycotic or post-traumatic. US screening guidelines recommend a one-time ultrasound for men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked. Measure outer wall to outer wall in the true transverse plane, document the relationship to the renal arteries, the maximum diameter, and iliac extension. Rupture risk rises with size; elective repair is commonly considered at about 5.5 cm in men (about 5.0 cm in women), with rapid growth (about 1 cm per year), or with symptoms. After endovascular repair, ultrasound surveillance looks for sac growth and endoleaks, of which type II, from lumbar arteries or the IMA, is the most common. Dissection shows a mobile intimal flap separating a true lumen, usually smaller with systolic forward flow, from a false lumen that may thrombose.
why it matters: Measurement technique is the heart of AAA questions: outer to outer, perpendicular to the long axis, never including only the patent lumen. Mural thrombus narrows the lumen but not the aneurysm. Trap: a tortuous aorta measured obliquely overestimates diameter. Trap two: a negative ultrasound does not exclude rupture, because retroperitoneal blood is hard to see; a hypotensive patient with a known AAA and back pain is an emergency. In dissection, Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta and needs surgery, while type B begins distal to the left subclavian.
on the registry: Expect questions on the AAA size definition, measurement method, repair threshold, most common endoleak type, and the features that separate true and false lumens.
checkpoint: Measure outer to outer; type II endoleak is the most common

title: IVC and Hepatic Veins
front clue: The IVC breathes with the patient; a fat, still IVC means the right heart is backed up
core concept: The IVC lies to the right of the aorta, receives the renal veins and hepatic veins, and enters the right atrium. It is thin walled and changes caliber with respiration and cardiac pulsation; it normally narrows with inspiration (sniff) and widens with Valsalva. A dilated IVC that collapses less than about 50 percent with a sniff suggests elevated right atrial pressure, as in right heart failure or tricuspid regurgitation. The three hepatic veins drain into the IVC just below the diaphragm. Normal hepatic venous Doppler is triphasic or multiphasic: two antegrade waves toward the heart (systolic S and diastolic D) and a small reversed atrial a wave, reflecting right heart events. Tricuspid regurgitation and right heart failure produce exaggerated pulsatility with reversal of the S wave; cirrhosis and other stiff livers dampen the waveform toward flat. Budd-Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction from thrombus, webs, or compression; findings include absent, reversed, or flat hepatic venous flow, intrahepatic collaterals, caudate hypertrophy, and ascites.
why it matters: Hepatic venous waveforms are a window onto the right heart, so reason from cardiac physiology: anything raising right atrial pressure exaggerates pulsatility, while anything stiffening the liver dampens it. Trap: a flat hepatic venous waveform can mean cirrhosis, but also Budd-Chiari or extrinsic compression, so check patency and flow direction. Trap two: do not mistake the reversed a wave of a normal waveform for pathology. The caudate lobe enlarges in Budd-Chiari because its own veins drain directly into the IVC and are often spared.
on the registry: Questions describe hepatic venous or IVC Doppler findings and ask for the cause (heart failure, tricuspid regurgitation, cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari) or the normal respiratory response.
checkpoint: Pulsatile hepatic veins point to the heart; flat ones point to the liver

title: Renal Artery Stenosis Doppler
front clue: Fast at the narrowing, slow and late beyond it
core concept: Renal artery stenosis is a cause of secondary hypertension, suspected in severe, resistant, or new-onset hypertension and in renal function that worsens on ACE inhibitors. Atherosclerosis, usually at the ostium or proximal segment, affects older patients; fibromuscular dysplasia affects young to middle-aged women, involves the mid to distal artery, and causes a string-of-beads appearance. The exam is performed after fasting, often in the morning with angle correction of 60 degrees or less. Direct criteria at the stenosis include a renal artery peak systolic velocity above about 180 to 200 cm/s and a renal to aortic velocity ratio (RAR) above about 3.5, both commonly used for stenosis of 60 percent or more. The RAR is less reliable when aortic velocity is unusually high or low. Indirect criteria in the intrarenal segmental arteries reflect a significant upstream stenosis: tardus parvus waveform, acceleration time above about 0.07 s, loss of the early systolic peak, and asymmetric resistive indices. Absent flow and a small kidney under about 8 to 9 cm suggest occlusion.
why it matters: Direct and indirect criteria work as a pair. The jet at the narrowing is fast; the flow beyond it is delayed and damped because the stenosis acts like a filter. If the main artery cannot be seen, intrarenal tardus parvus can still reveal a significant stenosis. Trap: velocities from a poorly angle-corrected or angle above 60 degrees signal are unreliable. Trap two: thresholds vary between labs, so learn the commonly taught values and the concept of the ratio, which corrects for overall cardiac output. Young woman with hypertension suggests fibromuscular dysplasia.
on the registry: Expect questions on direct versus indirect criteria, the renal to aortic ratio, the typical patient and location for fibromuscular dysplasia, and the meaning of a tardus parvus waveform.
checkpoint: RAR above 3.5 and PSV above about 180 to 200 point to significant stenosis

title: Retroperitoneal Masses and Fibrosis
front clue: Lymphoma lifts the aorta off the spine; fibrosis wraps it without lifting
core concept: The retroperitoneum contains the kidneys, adrenals, ureters, aorta, IVC, most of the pancreas, the second to fourth parts of the duodenum, and the ascending and descending colon. Retroperitoneal masses displace these structures anteriorly, a key sign of origin. Primary retroperitoneal tumors are mostly malignant, with liposarcoma most common, followed by leiomyosarcoma. Lymphadenopathy appears as hypoechoic, round or confluent masses around the aorta and IVC; bulky nodes can surround and lift the aorta away from the spine (floating aorta). Mesenteric nodes encasing mesenteric vessels can give a sandwich sign. Lymphoma is the classic cause, along with metastatic testicular, cervical, and prostate cancer; testicular cancer spreads first to para-aortic nodes near the renal hilum. Retroperitoneal fibrosis forms a hypoechoic, smooth plaque of tissue around the lower aorta and iliac vessels that encases them and draws the ureters medially, causing hydronephrosis, but does not usually displace the aorta anteriorly. Causes include idiopathic (often IgG4-related) disease, drugs, and malignancy. Retroperitoneal hematoma follows anticoagulation, trauma, or rupture.
why it matters: The tested reasoning is location and displacement. Ask what direction structures are pushed: anterior displacement means a retroperitoneal origin. Then separate lymphoma from fibrosis: lymphoma lifts the aorta and can be bulky and lobulated; fibrosis plasters around the aorta and pulls the ureters inward. Trap: a horseshoe kidney isthmus can mimic a para-aortic mass, so trace it to both kidneys. Trap two: testicular cancer spreads to nodes near the renal hila, not to inguinal nodes, because of its lymphatic drainage.
on the registry: Questions describe periaortic tissue or a displacing mass and ask for the most likely diagnosis, the direction of displacement, or the complication on the ureters.
checkpoint: Anterior displacement means retroperitoneal origin; medial ureters mean fibrosis

title: Bowel Wall Layers and IBD
front clue: Five layers, bright-dark-bright-dark-bright, from lumen outward
core concept: Normal bowel shows a gut signature of five alternating layers from the lumen outward: an echogenic superficial mucosal interface, hypoechoic deep mucosa (muscularis mucosae), echogenic submucosa, hypoechoic muscularis propria, and echogenic serosa. Normal wall thickness is about 3 mm or less in distended bowel and up to about 5 mm when collapsed. Thickened bowel in cross-section produces a target or doughnut appearance, and in long axis a pseudokidney sign; both are nonspecific and seen with tumor, inflammation, infection, ischemia, or edema. Crohn disease classically affects the terminal ileum with skip lesions, causing transmural wall thickening, hyperemia, echogenic inflamed mesenteric fat (creeping fat), strictures, fistulas, and abscesses. Ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum and spreads continuously proximally, mainly affecting the mucosa. Small bowel obstruction shows fluid-filled loops dilated beyond about 2.5 to 3 cm, with to-and-fro or absent peristalsis; the valvulae conniventes create a keyboard pattern. Graded compression with a linear transducer displaces normal gas-filled bowel to reveal deeper pathology.
why it matters: The layer pattern is a frequent recall item, so memorize it as alternating bright and dark starting bright at the lumen. Preservation of layers favors inflammation, while loss of layering suggests tumor, severe ischemia, or perforation. Trap: a target sign in the bowel means wall thickening, not a liver metastasis pattern; context separates them. Trap two: normal collapsed bowel can appear thick, so measure in distended segments. Transmural involvement and terminal ileum location favor Crohn disease; continuous rectal involvement favors ulcerative colitis.
on the registry: Questions ask for the order of the five layers, the meaning of target and pseudokidney signs, or the features that suggest Crohn disease.
checkpoint: Bright mucosal interface, dark muscularis mucosae, bright submucosa, dark muscularis propria, bright serosa

title: Acute Appendicitis
front clue: Noncompressible, blind-ending, over 6 mm: the appendix is guilty
core concept: Acute appendicitis usually results from luminal obstruction, often by an appendicolith or lymphoid hyperplasia. Patients have periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant at McBurney point, fever, nausea, and leukocytosis. Ultrasound uses graded compression with a high-frequency linear transducer to displace bowel. The inflamed appendix is a blind-ending, noncompressible tubular structure arising from the cecum, with an outer diameter over 6 mm, and it shows a target appearance in cross-section. Supporting findings include an appendicolith (echogenic and shadowing), wall hyperemia on color Doppler, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, periappendiceal fluid, and point tenderness directly over the appendix. Perforation is suggested by loss of the echogenic submucosal layer, a periappendiceal abscess or complex collection, and extraluminal appendicolith. A retrocecal appendix can be hard to see. In pregnancy the appendix is displaced upward by the uterus. In women, the differential includes ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, and tubo-ovarian abscess, so the pelvis should also be imaged.
why it matters: Size alone is not enough: a normal appendix can measure close to 6 mm, so noncompressibility, blind ending, and secondary inflammatory signs are combined. Proving the structure is blind ending separates appendix from terminal ileum, which is peristaltic and connects to the cecum. Trap: a nonvisualized appendix does not exclude appendicitis; it is an indeterminate result. Trap two: a perforated appendix may become compressible or decompressed, so look for abscess and fluid. Ultrasound is first choice in children and pregnancy to avoid radiation.
on the registry: Expect a vignette with right lower quadrant pain describing a tubular structure, asking for the diagnosis, the size threshold, the scanning technique, or signs of perforation.
checkpoint: Over 6 mm, noncompressible, blind ending, with or without an appendicolith

title: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
front clue: First-born boy, 3 to 6 weeks, projectile nonbilious vomiting: measure the pylorus
core concept: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is thickening of the pyloric muscle that obstructs gastric outflow. It usually presents between about 2 and 8 weeks of age, peaking around 3 to 6 weeks, more often in first-born males, with projectile nonbilious vomiting, dehydration, and a hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. A palpable olive-shaped mass may be felt in the epigastrium. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear transducer, often after giving the infant some fluid and placing the infant right side down, shows a persistently thickened and elongated pylorus. Commonly used criteria are a single muscle wall thickness of 3 mm or more and a channel length of about 15 to 17 mm or more. The thickened pylorus produces a target or doughnut sign in cross-section and a cervix sign in long axis, with redundant mucosa protruding into the antrum (antral nipple sign). Fluid fails to pass through the channel over several minutes of observation. Pylorospasm mimics stenosis but the muscle relaxes and fluid passes during the exam. Treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy.
why it matters: The muscle thickness measurement is the most testable number, so measure only the hypoechoic muscle, not the mucosa. Watching over time is crucial: true stenosis does not open, whereas pylorospasm intermittently does. Trap: bilious vomiting suggests obstruction beyond the ampulla, such as malrotation with volvulus, a surgical emergency, not pyloric stenosis. Trap two: an overdistended stomach pushes the pylorus posteriorly and makes it hard to see; placing the infant right side down or decompressing helps. Gas in the antrum can obscure the channel.
on the registry: Questions give an infant vignette with vomiting and ask for the diagnosis, the measurement thresholds, the significance of bilious vomiting, or how to separate pylorospasm.
checkpoint: Muscle 3 mm, channel about 15 to 17 mm; nonbilious projectile vomiting

title: Intussusception
front clue: Toddler with colicky pain and currant jelly stool: look for rings in the right abdomen
core concept: Intussusception is telescoping of a proximal bowel segment (intussusceptum) into a distal segment (intussuscipiens). It most often affects children between about 6 months and 3 years, peaking under 2 years, and is usually ileocolic and idiopathic, related to lymphoid hyperplasia. The classic triad is intermittent colicky abdominal pain, a palpable sausage-shaped mass, and red currant jelly stool, though all three are often absent. Ultrasound is the first imaging test. In cross-section the mass shows a target or doughnut sign of multiple concentric rings, typically 3 cm or more in diameter, usually in the right abdomen or subhepatic region; in long axis it shows a pseudokidney or sandwich appearance. Trapped mesenteric fat and lymph nodes within the mass are common. Small bowel intussusceptions are smaller, often transient, and usually reduce on their own. In older children and adults, a pathologic lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, polyp, or lymphoma should be sought. Treatment of ileocolic intussusception is image-guided air or hydrostatic enema reduction, unless there is perforation or peritonitis.
why it matters: Age and location are the reasoning shortcuts. A large target in the right abdomen of a toddler is ileocolic intussusception; a small transient target in the left or periumbilical region is likely a self-limited small bowel intussusception. Trap: a pseudokidney sign can be confused with a kidney, so look for the actual kidney nearby. Trap two: trapped fluid within the mass and absent flow suggest ischemia and lower the chance of successful enema reduction. Signs of perforation, such as free air or peritonitis, are contraindications to enema reduction.
on the registry: Expect pediatric vignettes asking for the diagnosis, the most common type and location, the sonographic sign, or a finding that predicts failed enema reduction.
checkpoint: Ileocolic, right side, 6 months to 3 years, multiple concentric rings

title: Ascites and Abscess
front clue: Clean fluid floats bowel freely; dirty fluid with septa and matted bowel suggests infection or cancer
core concept: Free peritoneal fluid collects in the most dependent spaces: in a supine patient, the hepatorenal space (Morison pouch) in the upper abdomen and the pelvis (rectouterine or rectovesical pouch), which is the most dependent overall. Other spaces include the subphrenic spaces, paracolic gutters, and splenorenal recess. Transudative ascites, from cirrhosis, heart failure, or renal failure, is usually anechoic with freely floating bowel loops. Exudative ascites, from infection, inflammation, or malignancy, more often contains debris, septations, or loculations, with matted or tethered bowel and possibly peritoneal nodules or omental caking. Hemoperitoneum may be echogenic, with clotted blood near the bleeding source (sentinel clot). An abscess is a localized collection with a thick irregular wall, internal debris, possibly gas with dirty shadowing or ring-down, and no internal flow, often with surrounding hyperemia. Common sites are subphrenic, subhepatic, pelvic, and interloop, frequently after surgery, appendicitis, diverticulitis, or Crohn disease. The FAST exam screens trauma patients for free fluid in the right and left upper quadrants, pelvis, and pericardium.
why it matters: Location tells you where to look, and content tells you what the fluid probably is. Always check Morison pouch and the pelvis first for small volumes. Septations and matted bowel are clues to an exudate, particularly malignancy, while anechoic fluid with floating bowel suggests a transudate, though this is not definitive and only fluid analysis is. Trap: a fluid-filled bowel loop can mimic a collection, so watch for peristalsis. Trap two: echogenic acute blood can be missed if you only look for anechoic fluid.
on the registry: Questions ask for the most dependent space, the features of transudate versus exudate, abscess appearance, or the FAST windows.
checkpoint: Morison pouch is the dependent upper abdomen; the pelvis is the most dependent overall

title: Abdominal Wall Hernias and Masses
front clue: Ask the patient to bear down: hernias move, most masses do not
core concept: A hernia is protrusion of fat or bowel through a defect, best demonstrated with dynamic imaging during Valsalva or standing with a linear transducer. Indirect inguinal hernias, the most common type, pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follow the spermatic cord, sometimes into the scrotum. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through the Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, are more common in women, and have a high risk of strangulation. Other types are umbilical, ventral, incisional, and Spigelian (at the lateral border of the rectus muscle along the semilunar line). Reducible hernias return with pressure; incarcerated ones do not. Strangulation is suggested by thick-walled, aperistaltic bowel, free fluid within the sac, and absent wall flow. Abdominal wall masses include lipoma (compressible, avascular, iso- to hyperechoic with thin echogenic lines), rectus sheath hematoma (with anticoagulation or coughing), desmoid tumor, and scar endometrioma, which causes cyclic pain at a cesarean scar.
why it matters: The inferior epigastric vessels are the landmark: lateral is indirect, medial is direct, and below the inguinal ligament is femoral. A dynamic maneuver is essential because a hernia may reduce at rest and be missed. Trap: femoral hernias are less common than inguinal hernias even in women, yet carry the higher strangulation risk. Trap two: a rectus sheath hematoma below the arcuate line can cross the midline because the posterior sheath is absent there. Cyclic pain at a cesarean scar points to endometrioma rather than hernia.
on the registry: Expect questions on landmarks that separate indirect, direct, and femoral hernias, signs of strangulation, and typical abdominal wall masses.
checkpoint: Lateral to inferior epigastrics is indirect; medial is direct; below the ligament is femoral

title: Thyroid Anatomy and Thyroiditis
front clue: Hashimoto is heterogeneous and dark; Graves is big and on fire
core concept: The thyroid has two lobes joined by an isthmus anterior to the trachea; each lobe is about 4 to 6 cm long and up to about 2 cm in anteroposterior and transverse dimensions. Normal parenchyma is homogeneous and more echogenic than the strap muscles anteriorly and the longus colli posteriorly. The common carotid artery and internal jugular vein lie lateral to each lobe, and the esophagus may be seen posterior to the left lobe, where it can mimic a nodule. A pyramidal lobe may arise from the isthmus. Hashimoto thyroiditis, the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions, produces an enlarged or later small gland with heterogeneous, hypoechoic, micronodular texture and echogenic fibrous septa; vascularity varies. It raises the risk of thyroid lymphoma. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism with a diffusely enlarged, often hypoechoic gland and marked hypervascularity (thyroid inferno) with high velocities. Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and causes a tender gland with patchy, ill-defined hypoechoic areas and reduced flow.
why it matters: Thyroiditis questions combine labs, symptoms, and Doppler. High vascularity with hyperthyroidism points to Graves; painful gland after a viral illness with low flow points to subacute thyroiditis; heterogeneous micronodular gland with hypothyroidism points to Hashimoto. Trap: the esophagus behind the left lobe can be mistaken for a nodule; ask the patient to swallow. Trap two: a thyroid inferno can also occur early in Hashimoto, so clinical context matters. Background thyroiditis makes nodule assessment harder because pseudonodules are common.
on the registry: Questions describe gland texture, vascularity, and symptoms and ask for the type of thyroiditis, or test normal anatomy and mimics such as the esophagus.
checkpoint: Graves: inferno; Hashimoto: micronodules and septa; de Quervain: painful and quiet

title: Thyroid Nodules and TI-RADS
front clue: Add the points: solid, very dark, taller than wide, irregular, punctate foci
core concept: ACR TI-RADS scores a nodule in five feature groups and adds the points. Composition: cystic or spongiform 0, mixed cystic and solid 1, solid or almost completely solid 2. Echogenicity: anechoic 0, hyperechoic or isoechoic 1, hypoechoic 2, very hypoechoic 3. Shape: wider than tall 0, taller than wide 3. Margin: smooth or ill-defined 0, lobulated or irregular 2, extrathyroidal extension 3. Echogenic foci: none or large comet-tail artifacts 0, macrocalcifications 1, peripheral rim calcifications 2, punctate echogenic foci 3 (points in this category are added for each type present). Total points set the level: TR1 0 points benign, TR2 2 points not suspicious, TR3 3 points mildly suspicious, TR4 4 to 6 moderately suspicious, TR5 7 or more highly suspicious. FNA thresholds are 2.5 cm for TR3, 1.5 cm for TR4, and 1 cm for TR5, with follow-up for smaller nodules at 1.5, 1.0, and 0.5 cm respectively. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, often solid, hypoechoic, with punctate echogenic foci.
why it matters: Most TI-RADS questions are scoring exercises, so practice adding points from a verbal description. Size thresholds only apply after the level is set. Trap: large comet-tail artifacts in a cystic nodule indicate colloid and score zero, whereas punctate echogenic foci without comet tails score three. Trap two: taller than wide is assessed in the transverse plane only. A spongiform nodule is benign and scores zero for composition, and the other features should not be added on top of it. Very hypoechoic means darker than strap muscle, not just darker than thyroid.
on the registry: Expect a nodule described in words, asking for its TI-RADS point total or level, whether FNA is indicated at a given size, or which feature is most suspicious.
checkpoint: TR3 FNA at 2.5 cm, TR4 at 1.5 cm, TR5 at 1 cm

title: Parathyroid, Neck Nodes and Salivary Glands
front clue: Oval, hypoechoic, behind the thyroid with a polar artery: parathyroid adenoma
core concept: There are usually four parathyroid glands posterior to the thyroid; normal glands are too small to see. A parathyroid adenoma, the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism with high calcium and parathyroid hormone, is an oval, homogeneous, hypoechoic mass posterior or inferior to the thyroid, separated from it by an echogenic line, often with a polar feeding artery. Normal cervical lymph nodes are oval with an echogenic fatty hilum and hilar flow. Suspicious nodes are round (short-to-long axis ratio above about 0.5), lose the fatty hilum, show peripheral or chaotic flow, or contain microcalcifications or cystic change, features typical of papillary thyroid carcinoma metastases. The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland, drained by the Stensen duct; the submandibular gland, drained by the Wharton duct, is the most common site of salivary stones. Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary tumor, usually parotid; Warthin tumor is the second most common, often in older male smokers, and can be bilateral. Sialadenitis causes an enlarged hypoechoic hypervascular gland.
why it matters: For a posterior neck lesion, decide whether it is thyroid, parathyroid, or node. The echogenic line separating it from the thyroid and a polar artery favor parathyroid; an echogenic hilum favors a benign node. Trap: a posterior thyroid nodule can mimic an adenoma, so look for the separating capsule. Trap two: loss of the fatty hilum in a reactive node can occur, so combine several features. Submandibular stones are more common than parotid stones because Wharton duct secretions are thicker and flow uphill.
on the registry: Questions describe a neck mass and ask whether it is parathyroid, node, or salivary in origin, or test the most common salivary tumor and stone site.
checkpoint: Benign node has a fatty hilum; submandibular gland is the stone gland

title: Acute Scrotum
front clue: Teen with sudden pain and no flow: torsion; adult with hyperemic epididymis: epididymitis
core concept: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, most common in adolescents and often related to a bell-clapper deformity, in which the testis lacks normal posterior fixation. It presents with sudden severe pain, nausea, and an absent cremasteric reflex. Ultrasound shows absent or reduced intratesticular flow compared with the normal side, an enlarged testis that becomes heterogeneous and hypoechoic with time, and a twisted spermatic cord (whirlpool sign). Doppler should be optimized for slow flow (low PRF, low wall filter, appropriate gain) and always compared with the contralateral testis. Partial torsion or spontaneous detorsion may leave some flow. Salvage is high within about 6 hours and falls sharply after 12 to 24 hours, so this is a surgical emergency. Epididymitis is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in adults; the epididymis, especially the head, is enlarged, hypoechoic, and hyperemic, with reactive hydrocele and wall thickening. Spread to the testis (orchitis) makes it hyperemic. Torsion of the appendix testis affects prepubertal boys, with a small avascular nodule.
why it matters: Doppler comparison is everything: decreased flow is torsion, increased flow is inflammation. Always set slow-flow settings on the normal side first, then compare. Trap: flow does not exclude torsion, because partial or intermittent torsion may preserve some signal, so a twisted cord or asymmetry still matters. Trap two: rebound hyperemia after spontaneous detorsion can mimic orchitis. Time from symptom onset guides urgency, and imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.
on the registry: Expect vignettes with scrotal pain, age, and Doppler findings, asking for the diagnosis, the best Doppler setting, or the time window for salvage.
checkpoint: Decreased flow is torsion; increased flow is epididymo-orchitis

title: Testicular Masses and Varicocele
front clue: Inside the testis assume cancer; outside the testis assume benign
core concept: A solid intratesticular mass is considered malignant until proven otherwise, and most are germ cell tumors. Seminoma is the most common pure germ cell tumor, peaking in the fourth decade, and appears as a homogeneous hypoechoic mass. Nonseminomatous and mixed tumors occur in younger men and are heterogeneous with cystic areas and calcifications. Tumor markers include AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH. Lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men over about 60 and is often bilateral. Extratesticular masses are usually benign: epididymal cysts and spermatoceles, hydroceles, and the adenomatoid tumor, the most common extratesticular neoplasm. Testicular microlithiasis shows tiny nonshadowing echogenic foci, commonly defined as five or more per image. A varicocele is dilation of the pampiniform plexus veins above about 2 to 3 mm with reflux during Valsalva. It is left sided in most cases because the left gonadal vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein. A new right-sided or nondecompressing varicocele should prompt a search for an abdominal mass.
why it matters: Location is the first branch point: intratesticular solid means likely cancer and urology referral; extratesticular cystic means likely benign. Then use age: seminoma in the thirties, nonseminoma in the twenties, lymphoma after sixty. Trap: a varicocele can be missed if the patient is not scanned with Valsalva or standing. Trap two: an isolated right varicocele is unusual because the right gonadal vein drains obliquely into the IVC, so it may indicate a mass. Testicular cancer spreads first to retroperitoneal nodes near the renal hila.
on the registry: Questions describe a scrotal mass by location, age, and echogenicity and ask for the diagnosis, or test why varicoceles favor the left side.
checkpoint: Seminoma is homogeneous and hypoechoic; varicocele is left sided and grows with Valsalva

title: Prostate Basics
front clue: Cancer starts in the peripheral zone; BPH grows in the transition zone
core concept: The prostate lies below the bladder, surrounding the proximal urethra, and is evaluated transabdominally through a full bladder or more accurately by transrectal ultrasound. The zonal anatomy includes the peripheral zone, which forms about 70 percent of the glandular tissue in young men and gives rise to about 70 percent of prostate cancers; the transition zone, around the urethra, which is the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia; and the central zone, around the ejaculatory ducts. The seminal vesicles lie posterior and superior to the gland. Normal gland weight is about 20 to 25 grams, and volume is estimated with the ellipsoid formula, length times width times height times about 0.52. Benign prostatic hyperplasia enlarges the transition zone, often with calcifications and nodules, and can elevate the bladder base, causing bladder outlet obstruction, a thick trabeculated bladder wall, and increased post-void residual. Prostate cancer may appear as a hypoechoic peripheral zone lesion, but many are isoechoic, so ultrasound is mainly used to guide biopsy. PSA is the screening blood test.
why it matters: Zonal anatomy is the most frequently tested prostate fact: peripheral zone for cancer, transition zone for BPH. Transabdominal scans in the abdomen exam mainly show gland size and its effect on the bladder. Trap: many prostate cancers are isoechoic and invisible on ultrasound, so a normal-looking gland does not exclude cancer. Trap two: an enlarged median lobe can project into the bladder and mimic a bladder mass; trace it to the prostate. The volume formula is the same one used for the bladder and other organs.
on the registry: Expect questions on zonal anatomy, the site of BPH and cancer, the volume formula, and the bladder findings of outlet obstruction.
checkpoint: Peripheral zone cancer, transition zone BPH

title: Patient Preparation and Infection Control
front clue: NPO for the gallbladder, full bladder for the pelvis, clean hands for everyone
core concept: Adult abdominal and gallbladder exams usually require fasting for about 6 to 8 hours to distend the gallbladder and reduce bowel gas. Aorta and mesenteric or renal artery Doppler studies are also performed fasting, often in the morning. Renal exams usually need no fasting, but a full bladder helps evaluate the bladder and distal ureters, and pelvic exams use a full bladder as a window. Standard precautions apply to every patient, and hand hygiene before and after contact is the single most important infection-control measure. Alcohol hand rub is not reliable against Clostridioides difficile spores, so soap and water are used. Transmission-based precautions add contact (gown and gloves, as for MRSA or C. difficile), droplet (surgical mask), or airborne (N95 respirator and negative-pressure room, as for tuberculosis) measures. Under the Spaulding classification, transducers on intact skin are noncritical and need low-level disinfection; endocavitary probes on mucous membranes are semicritical and need high-level disinfection plus a probe cover; procedures through broken skin require a sterile cover and sterile gel.
why it matters: Preparation questions test the reason behind each instruction: fasting distends the gallbladder and reduces gas; a full bladder displaces bowel and creates a window. Infection questions test matching: precaution type to organism, and disinfection level to probe use. Trap: a probe cover does not replace high-level disinfection for endocavitary transducers. Trap two: gloves do not replace hand hygiene. A nonfasting patient with a contracted gallbladder should be rescheduled or documented, not reported as abnormal.
on the registry: Questions ask for the correct prep for a given exam, the disinfection level for a probe type, or the precaution type for a named infection.
checkpoint: Intact skin low-level, mucous membrane high-level, broken skin sterile

title: Ultrasound-Guided Biopsy and Paracentesis
front clue: In plane shows the whole needle; out of plane shows only a dot
core concept: Before an ultrasound-guided procedure, the team obtains informed consent, reviews coagulation status and anticoagulant use, confirms the site, and performs a time-out. Sterile technique uses a sterile transducer cover and sterile gel. In the in-plane (long-axis) approach, the needle travels within the beam and its entire shaft and tip are visible. In the out-of-plane (short-axis) approach the needle crosses the beam and appears as an echogenic dot, so the tip must be tracked carefully. Needle visibility improves when the needle is more perpendicular to the beam, with beam steering or needle-enhancement software. Fine-needle aspiration yields cells for cytology; core biopsy yields tissue for histology. Bleeding is the most common significant complication, and color Doppler helps avoid vessels and check for post-procedure hematoma. For paracentesis, choose the largest pocket of fluid free of bowel, usually in a lower quadrant lateral to the rectus sheath, and use color Doppler to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels. For thoracentesis, the needle passes just above a rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle.
why it matters: Expect questions about safety and visualization. The in-plane approach shows the tip continuously, which reduces the risk of passing beyond the target; out of plane, the dot you see may be the shaft rather than the tip. Steep needle angles are hard to see because sound reflects away from the transducer. Trap: the inferior epigastric vessels run within the rectus sheath, so punctures through the rectus muscle risk bleeding. Trap two: the time-out happens right before the procedure begins, not only at registration.
on the registry: Questions test in-plane versus out-of-plane visualization, needle visibility, pre-procedure steps, paracentesis site selection, and complications.
checkpoint: Paracentesis lateral to the rectus, needle above the rib for thoracentesis

title: Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Basics
front clue: Microbubbles stay in the vessels and are imaged at low MI
core concept: Ultrasound contrast agents are gas-filled microbubbles, typically a perfluorocarbon or sulfur hexafluoride gas in a lipid or protein shell, small enough to cross capillaries. They are purely intravascular (blood pool) agents, unlike CT and MRI contrast, which leak into the interstitium. They are excreted by exhaling the gas through the lungs, are not nephrotoxic, involve no ionizing radiation, and can be used in renal failure. Imaging uses contrast-specific modes at a low mechanical index, commonly under about 0.2 to 0.3, so the bubbles oscillate nonlinearly and produce harmonic signals without being destroyed. Liver enhancement phases are arterial (about 10 to 30 seconds after injection), portal venous (about 30 to 120 seconds), and late (after about 120 seconds until the bubbles clear). Hemangioma shows peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in; HCC typically shows arterial phase hyperenhancement with late, mild washout after about 60 seconds; metastases and non-HCC malignancies wash out early or markedly. Serious allergic reactions are rare, and resuscitation equipment and trained staff should be available.
why it matters: The key concepts are that bubbles stay in the blood pool and that low MI preserves them. Washout timing and degree separate HCC from other malignancies, and the CEUS LI-RADS system formalizes this. Trap: microbubbles do not cause contrast nephropathy, so kidney function is not a barrier. Trap two: a high MI destroys bubbles, so CEUS images look poor if the MI is left at standard settings. Contraindications are mainly known hypersensitivity to the agent or its components.
on the registry: Expect questions on bubble composition, why low MI is used, vascular phases, enhancement patterns of liver lesions, and safety in renal failure.
checkpoint: Blood pool agent, low MI, not nephrotoxic

title: Scanning Protocols and Measurement Technique
front clue: Two planes, the right position, calipers on the right walls
core concept: A complete abdominal protocol documents every organ in at least two planes, with labels for side, organ, and position. Patient positioning changes the window: left lateral decubitus brings the liver and gallbladder down from the ribs and moves stones; right lateral decubitus opens a coronal window to the spleen and left kidney; upright or prone views confirm stone mobility; deep inspiration lowers the liver and spleen. Measurement rules are tested repeatedly: the aorta outer wall to outer wall, perpendicular to the vessel; the common bile duct inner wall to inner wall; the gallbladder wall on the anterior wall perpendicular to the beam; the kidney at its maximal long axis. Volumes of the bladder, prostate, and other organs use the ellipsoid formula, length times width times height times about 0.52. For Doppler, keep the angle of insonation at 60 degrees or less, align the angle correction cursor parallel to the vessel wall or flow, size the sample volume to the vessel, and set the scale to avoid aliasing.
why it matters: Protocol questions reward knowing why a step exists. Two planes reduce the chance that an artifact is mistaken for pathology. Measuring perpendicular to the structure avoids oblique overestimation. Doppler angles above 60 degrees magnify velocity errors, so they produce unreliable peak velocities. Trap: the anterior gallbladder wall is measured because the posterior wall is affected by posterior enhancement. Trap two: incomplete documentation of the whole organ, especially the kidney poles or the distal aorta, is a common protocol failure.
on the registry: Questions ask for correct caliper placement, the best patient position for a structure, the volume formula, or Doppler technique errors.
checkpoint: Aorta outer to outer, ducts inner to inner, Doppler angle 60 or less

title: Critical Findings Communication
front clue: Emergent findings need a direct call, documented with who, when and how
core concept: Some findings require urgent action and must be communicated directly and promptly to the responsible provider, following the ACR practice parameter and the institution's policy. Examples in abdominal and superficial ultrasound include ruptured or symptomatic aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, free fluid in an unstable trauma patient, testicular torsion, hepatic artery thrombosis or renal vein thrombosis in a transplant, emphysematous or gangrenous cholecystitis, and strangulated hernia. The sonographer's role is to recognize the finding, notify the interpreting physician immediately according to protocol, and stay with or monitor the patient as needed; the sonographer does not give a diagnosis to the patient. Communication is usually verbal, by phone or in person, rather than relying on a written report, and documentation includes the name of the person notified, the date and time, and the method. Patient privacy rules (HIPAA) limit who may receive results. If a patient becomes unstable during the exam, such as with syncope, chest pain, or hypotension, stop the exam, call for help, and follow the emergency protocol.
why it matters: Scope of practice is the heart of these questions. The sonographer recognizes and escalates, the physician interprets and decides, and everything is documented. Trap: telling a patient they have cancer, torsion, or an aneurysm is outside the sonographer's scope even if the finding is obvious; the right action is to reassure and escalate. Trap two: leaving a message or relying on the final report is not adequate for an emergent finding; a direct conversation with the responsible provider is expected. Patient safety comes before completing the protocol.
on the registry: Expect scenario questions asking what the sonographer should do first when an emergent finding is seen, what to document, or what may be told to the patient.
checkpoint: Recognize, notify directly, document who, when and how; never diagnose to the patient
